## 📄 Reading a document from Commons

**Two archives, one reader.** The card on the left is a **329-page PDF** on Wikimedia Commons (`The Three Hostages`, 1924, credited "From internet archive"); the one beside it is a **DjVu** — the format Wikisource prefers — and on the right an **Internet Archive book**. All three are the same widget underneath: turn, zoom, jump to a page, and **facing pages**.

**Commons documents bring their own rules**, all measured:

- the page count and the page renders come from **one API call** (`imageinfo`); a 329-page book costs the same as a 2-page one;
- page renders are only served at certain **widths** — 120, 250, 330, 500, 960, 1280 work, and asking for a "round" 400/640/700/800/1024 returns an error page that browsers refuse to show at all. The zoom ladder therefore offers the widths that exist, and stops at 960;
- **no text layer** unless Wikisource has proofread the file, so there is no search box here — that is a Commons fact, not a bug (the Internet Archive's books do have search-inside, via IIIF);
- **PNG export works**, because Wikimedia's page renders send CORS.

### …and where a Wikisource volunteer transcribed it

These are **the same widget** — the four document cards differ only in their `file`. Whether a card can show text is **detected from the file** (one check for `Page:`/`Index:` pages on a Wikisource), never configured: this one is transcribed and grows a **¶**, the others are not and have none.

**The same widget as the cards above** — the difference is the *file*, not the card: `"Homo Sum"` (38 pages, under a megabyte) has been transcribed page by page on **Wikisource** and is fully **Validated**, so its card grows a **¶ button**: press it and the page's text appears under its proofreading grade — *"en.wikisource · Validated"* — with a link to the transcription itself. **The grade is the point:** a volume that was only bulk-scanned shows *"Not proofread (uncorrected OCR)"* instead (we measured exactly that on a 1,208-page reference set that had never been human-checked), and a reader has to know which one they are quoting. A file with no transcription — the Mozart DjVu above — has no ¶ button at all.

The grey **Open the original** link under each card hands the file to your browser's own PDF viewer, which is where you want to be for printing or selecting text.
